newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS -- Prices not seen deterring Brazil farmers.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS -- Prices not seen deterring Brazil farmers.

text.p: The recent sharp drop in international soybean prices is unlikely to deter Brazilian farmers who should be starting plantings this month for the 1996/97 crop, traders and analysts said.
"The internal market has slipped back a little in line with Chicago this week but there is not much business so these are only nominal prices anyway," said Flavio Franca.
"What is more important are the problems of viability as far as the new crop is concerned, namely the shortage of credit and seeds," he added.

These problems could mean lower planted area than earlier expected in the centre-west states such as Mato Grosso but in the south of the country, farmers in the key producing regions such as Parana are even keener to plant soybeans, he said.
As a result total planted area Safras still anticipates will see a six percent rise to 11.4 million hectares.
This should mean an increase in the harvest to 26 million to 27 million tonnes against last year's 23.2 million.
Overseas analysts think the harvest may be even higher.

"Soybean prices are already over $1 above the level prevailing at this time last year, and the abolition of a 13 percent sales tax in Brazil means that producers will be gaining nearly $2 extra for every bushel of soybeans planted," London brokers GNI said in a recent market alert.
"GNI believes that planted acreage will in fact be significantly higher, giving a crop output of higher than 27.5 million tonnes," he said.
In the wait for the new crop, talk in the market is centred not so much on production but on imports and exports.
Earlier today U.S. traders cited talk of purchases by China of up 250,000 tonnes of soymeal, some of which possibly of South American origin.
Most traders in Brazil said that while China is always looking to buy when the market was on the way down, they had not heard of any concrete deals.
One however said he had heard up to 60,000 tonnes of soymeal had been sold ex-South America, 25,000 tonnes of which were Brazilian for delivery from October right through to January.
One other rumor circulating in the market was that Brazil had bought U.S. soybeans, with one dealer citing three cargoes for November/December delivery purchased by a large processor.
Brazil is expected to import around one million tonnes of soybeans during this crop year, principally from Paraguay.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
